The power went off halfway through the maths test review, and the fans slowed to a stop. Ms Pillai had ten minutes left before the bell and chalk dust stuck to everyone's arms.
“Quick. Seven eights. Hands up for fifty-four.”
Most of the class raised their hands. Pranav, at the front, shouted, “Fifty-four, obviously!”
Indu had written fifty-six. She had checked it twice, counting on her fingers under the desk. She looked at the sea of hands, then at her paper, and her hand crept up.
“It's fifty-six,” Ms Pillai said. A few groans. Indu stared at her own neat fifty-six, then rubbed it out and wrote it again, harder.

qa.q: What answer had Indu written?
qa.a: Indu had written fifty-six.

qa.q: Why did Indu's hand creep up for fifty-four?
qa.a: She felt unsure and uneasy seeing most hands up, so going with the group felt safer than being alone, even though she had checked twice.

qa.q: What small step could help Indu trust her working next time?
qa.a: She could keep her hand down and say quietly, "I got fifty-six, I checked it," or ask the teacher to use written answers so she isn't swayed by the room.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel when the answer was fifty-six?
qa.a: Pranav might feel embarrassed, having shouted "obviously" in front of everyone and been wrong.

grounding: Shows a child who knew the correct answer changing it because most of the class chose another, under heat and time pressure.

The coaching centre above the sweet shop in Pune smelled of samosas. Sir held up two stones. “A big one and a small one, dropped together from the roof, no wind. Which lands first?”
“The big one!” Suraj said, and nearly everyone agreed.
Yogesh had watched a video about this at home. They land together, he thought. He even remembered the experiment with a hammer and a feather.
“Yogesh?”
He looked around at the nodding heads. “The big one, sir,” he said.
Sir smiled. “Actually, they land at almost the same time.” Suraj shrugged. Yogesh looked down at his notebook, cheeks warm, wishing he could take the words back.

qa.q: Where was the coaching centre?
qa.a: It was above the sweet shop in Pune.

qa.q: How was Yogesh feeling after the teacher gave the answer?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and regretful; his cheeks were warm and he wished he could take his words back, because he had known they land together.

qa.q: What went wrong for Yogesh, and what might fix it?
qa.a: He let the nodding heads outweigh what he knew; next time he could say his answer and his reason, even if he's the only one.

qa.q: Why might Suraj react so differently to being wrong?
qa.a: Suraj just shrugged, having said an honest belief; Yogesh had gone against his own knowledge, which stings more.

grounding: Shows a child giving the class's answer instead of the one he was privately certain of, because being the lone voice felt harder.

“You told me yesterday the Moon doesn't make its own light,” Vaibhav said as they crossed the playground.
Sachin kicked a stone. “Yeah.”
“So why did you say it does? You were the last one Ma'am asked.”
“Everyone else said it does. Even Jyoti.”
Jyoti, walking ahead, turned round. “I just guessed!”
“See?” said Vaibhav. “She guessed. You knew.”
Sachin scuffed his shoe. “When all twenty say yes, you start thinking maybe you read it wrong. Being the only one sounds... weird.”
“You'd have been right, though.”
“I know,” Sachin muttered. “That's the worst part.”

qa.a: Sachin told Vaibhav the Moon doesn't make its own light.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he said "That's the worst part"?
qa.a: He felt frustrated with himself and a bit ashamed, because he had known the right answer and still gave it up.

qa.q: How could a teacher make it easier for Sachin to keep his answer?
qa.a: The teacher could ask everyone to write answers first before anyone speaks, so no one hears the crowd before deciding.

qa.q: What was it like for Jyoti to learn the guess swayed Sachin?
qa.a: Jyoti might feel surprised, maybe a little sorry, having only guessed and never meant anyone to follow.

grounding: Shows a child who changed a correct answer to match the class and later admits doubting himself felt easier than standing alone.
